newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croatia needs privatisation to seal success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croatia needs privatisation to seal success.

text.p: Recovering from a devastating four-year war, Croatia has achieved macroeconomic stability and now needs to push ahead with structural changes to secure stable long-term growth.
"It is important that our impressive macroeconomic results are transformed into the microeconomic sphere," said Economy Minister Davor Stern.

He said the government is committed, despite considerable public opposition, to going ahead more aggressively with the privatisation of key public sectors which remained untouched by the process launched in 1991.
An austerity programme started in October 1993 helped Croatia slash war-induced inflation of more than 1,000 percent to no more than 3.5 percent annually in 1996.
It also stabilised the exchange rate of the then domestic currency and paved the way for the introduction of the kuna at 3.7 to the German mark and six to the dollar in May 1994.

The aftermath of the war, combined with the loss of internal Yugoslav markets, reduced economic growth to a modest 0.8 percent in 1994. But the rebound in activity since has seen economic growth accelerate to 1.7 percent in 1995 and around six percent in 1996.
This rate of growth can be sustained only if privatisation, and with it competitiveness, accelerates, analysts say.

Croatia's private sector currently accounts for no more than between 50 and 60 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and the government has committed itself in a letter to the World Bank to complete the privatisation process by 1999.
STATE TO SELL MOST OF ITS REMAINING PORTFOLIO
As part of the privatisation drive, the state privatisation agency will sell $2.3 billion worth of assets, most of its remaining portfolio, through a mass voucher scheme to be launched in April.
The mass privatisation, encompassing roughly 800 firms, is expected to bring in badly needed capital and result in better management.
The latter could be provided by investment funds expected to manage the majority of small shareholders' portfolios, analysts said.
"It will take a year or two for the benefits of having a clear ownership structure to become evident," said Zarko Miljenovic, chief economist at Zagrebacka Banka.

Although industrial productivity in industry rose a formidable 11 percent in 1996, according to Miljenovic's data, this did not necessarily reflect the benefits of restructuring but was due largely to greater usage of idle capacity after a long recession.

Privatisation is also a necessary prerequisite for attracting badly needed direct foreign investment. This doubled to about $280 million in 1996 but is still small compared with other emerging economies.

In a recent case underlining the danger of not getting serious privatisation rolling, the U.S. corporation Levi Strauss told the leading Croatian textile firm Varteks that it would not extend its licence for Levi's jeans unless the firm was privatised by June.
GOVERNMENT HAS MIXED FEELINGS ABOUT SELLING SOME INDUSTRIES
Restructuring the banking sector and utilities, such as telecommunications, roads and railways, water, forestry and the country's biggest company, the oil and gas monopoly INA, is most problematic.
The government is often reluctant to let these sectors go for a mixture of economic and political reasons, even though analysts believe privatising them would benefit the economy.
"Long-term prospects for growth of the Croatian economy depend mostly on the privatisation of large state-owned banks and public utilities," Miljenovic said.

Although their contribution to the GDP is relatively small, the importance of utilities and banks is far larger because they influence the efficiency of the entire economy through the price of their services.
But Stern cited the example of nearby Hungary, where private foreign owners of utilities raised prices, to argue that such a sell-off could provoke a public outcry if it was carried out carelessly.

The government wants to offer 30 percent of seven utilities and INA to foreign investors, with the rest of the stake going to the state pension fund, public sector employees and citizens who could not take part in previous privatisation deals.

In the banking sector, the government overhauled three of the four large ailing state-owned banks -- -- Slavonska, Splitska and Rijecka, by taking over their bad debts and injecting funds into them last year.
Analysts believe they should be privatised to free them of the political pressures that led to careless lending in the past. The government has yet to spell out its intentions.
SOME SECTORS WILL STAY IN GOVERNMENT HANDS
The government says it wants to keep control of state television, the publishing company Narodne Novine and possibly the postal service and energy distribution.
Apart from political concerns, restructuring or privatisation of some huge state concerns, notably Croatian Railways, faces problems from a huge old debt burden and bloated workforce.

Others, including state telecommunications monopoly HPT, are among the most profitable Croatian companies and potentially interesting for foreign buyers, but the government does not want to rush into selling them, hoping for a better price in the future. However, the government has drafted a law which would split HPT into postal and telecommunications units, paving the way for their possible privatisation.
